answer_text:
Let \(P\in V\) be a nonzero polynomial, and let \(d=\deg P\).

The defining identity is

\[
P(X^3)=(X^{n+1}+1)P(X).
\]

Compare total degrees. Since

\[
\deg P(X^3)=3d
\]

and

\[
\deg\bigl((X^{n+1}+1)P(X)\bigr)=n+1+d,
\]

we must have

\[
3d=n+1+d,
\]

so

\[
2d=n+1.
\]

Thus

\[
d=\frac{n+1}{2}.
\]

If \(n\) is even, then \(\frac{n+1}{2}\) is not an integer, so no nonzero \(P\) exists. Hence \(V=\{0\}\) in that case.

Now suppose \(n\) is odd. Write

\[
n=2k-1,
\]

so \(n+1=2k\). Then any nonzero solution must have

\[
d=k.
\]

Thus we may write

\[
P(X)=a_0+a_1X+\cdots+a_kX^k
\]

with \(a_k\neq 0\).

Now compare the coefficient of \(X^j\) for \(1\le j\le k\). On the right-hand side,

\[
(X^{2k}+1)P(X)=P(X)+X^{2k}P(X),
\]

and the term \(X^{2k}P(X)\) has degree at least \(2k\), so it does not contribute to the coefficient of \(X^j\) for \(j\le k\). Therefore the coefficient of \(X^j\) on the right is simply \(a_j\).

On the left-hand side, \(P(X^3)\) has monomials \(a_iX^{3i}\), so the coefficient of \(X^j\) is

\[
\begin{cases}
a_{j/3}, & 3\mid j,\\
0, & 3\nmid j.
\end{cases}
\]

Hence for every \(1\le j\le k\),

\[
a_j=
\begin{cases}
a_{j/3}, & 3\mid j,\\
0, & 3\nmid j.
\end{cases}
\]

Now take any \(j\ge 1\). Write \(j=3^t m\), where \(3\nmid m\). Repeatedly applying the relation above gives

\[
a_j=a_m.
\]

But since \(3\nmid m\), the relation gives \(a_m=0\). Therefore \(a_j=0\) for every \(j\ge 1\). In particular,

\[
a_k=0,
\]

contradicting \(a_k\neq 0\).

So no nonzero polynomial \(P\) satisfies the identity, even when \(n\) is odd.

Therefore

\[
V=\{0\},
\]

and its dimension is

\[
\boxed{0}.
\]
